summary: Describes a framework for benchmarking the traffic management features of networking devices, such as policing and shaping. It aims to give repeatable tests that objectively compare devices using representative application traffic.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a fair race for network boxes that control traffic, with the same rules for everyone, so you can see which one does best.

questions: how to test traffic shaping and policing on network devices
how to test traffic shaping and policing
how to measure network device performance
what is the traffic management benchmarking framework
subtitle: A framework for testing how well network devices manage traffic rates.

tldr.problem: Network devices handle traffic policing, shaping and queuing differently, with no standard way to compare their performance.
tldr.mechanism: This framework defines repeatable tests and metrics for benchmarking traffic management features like policing (rate limiting), queuing, and shaping on network devices.
tldr.outcome: Equipment vendors and operators can now objectively compare how well devices manage traffic rates, both in isolation and under heavy load.

facts.label: Recommended test duration
facts.value: 60 seconds minimum (30 seconds for some tests)

today: RFC 7640 is an Informational RFC that provides a benchmarking framework but is not a standard specification. It has not been obsoleted and provides the only comprehensive framework for objectively comparing traffic management capabilities across different network devices.

sections.title: Introduction and Traffic Management Overview
sections.content:
Network devices manage traffic through five main functions: classification (sorting packets by rules like VLAN or DSCP), policing (dropping or remarking packets that exceed a rate limit), scheduling (queuing and ordering packets for transmission), shaping (smoothing bursty traffic to a configured rate), and active queue management (proactively dropping packets to prevent congestion).

Currently there is no standard way to benchmark these capabilities. Different manufacturers implement them differently, and operators have no objective way to compare devices. This framework fills that gap by defining repeatable test methods and metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: Network boxes do five things with traffic: sort it, limit it, queue it, smooth it, and drop it early if needed. Nobody had a fair test to compare which box does these best, so this RFC makes one.

sections.title: Test Setup and Traffic Patterns
sections.content:
Tests use either stateless traffic (UDP packets with sequence numbers and timestamps) or stateful traffic (TCP connections with realistic application patterns). A network delay emulator is required for TCP tests to emulate round-trip latency and allow TCP's window-based flow control to work properly.

The test setup consists of a transmitting host, the device under test, a network delay emulator, and a receiving host. Tests can be unidirectional or bidirectional. For TCP tests, the setup includes a passive delay element (a fiber spool is recommended) to add network latency without corrupting packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Tests send packets (either simple datagrams or real-looking TCP traffic) through the box while measuring what comes out the other side. A delay line makes sure TCP traffic acts like it came from far away.

sections.title: Metrics and Measurements
sections.content:
Stateless tests measure: Burst Size Achieved (the largest burst that passes without loss), Lost Packets and Out-of-Sequence packets, Packet Delay and Packet Delay Variation (the variation in one-way delays), and for shapers, the Shaper Rate (average output rate) and Shaper Burst Bytes (the size of trains of back-to-back packets).

Stateful TCP tests measure TCP Test Pattern Execution Time (how long an application scenario takes), TCP Efficiency (the percentage of bytes not retransmitted), and Buffer Delay (how much the round-trip time increased due to queuing).
sections.plainLanguage: The tests measure: Did packets arrive? In order? On time? With how much delay? For TCP, how fast did the fake application complete?

sections.title: Testing Individual Functions and Capacity
sections.content:
The framework divides tests into two categories: individual tests that benchmark a single traffic management function (such as testing one policer or queue), and capacity tests that stress multiple instances (many policers on one port, or one policer on all ports, or maximum policers on all ports).

For policing, tests send bursts matching the configured Committed Burst Size (CBS) and Excess Burst Size (EBS) at the Committed Information Rate (CIR) and Excess Information Rate (EIR), then measure what the device allows through. For queuing and shaping, tests send bursts matching the queue depth and measure lost packets, delay, and packet ordering.
sections.plainLanguage: First test one thing at a time: one policer, one queue. Then test if the box handles many at once. Each test sends known traffic and counts what gets through.

sections.title: Tools and Best Practices
sections.content:
The framework recommends hardware-based test equipment for high-speed links (1 Gigabit or faster). For lower speeds, open source tools like iperf (for UDP throughput) and netperf (for TCP request-response patterns) can be used, though they have software-based performance limits. The test device must be capable of generating traffic at line rate, controlling classification (IP addresses, DSCP), and measuring round-trip time and retransmissions.

Critical test parameters include the Test Duration (minimum 60 seconds, though 30 seconds is acceptable for some tests) and the Test Runs (minimum 10 runs to ensure repeatability). Results must report not just averages but the variability between runs.
sections.plainLanguage: Use real test equipment if you can afford it, or open-source software tools if not. Run each test at least 10 times and measure how consistent the results are.
